column2: Retain an inland administration, place its eastern possessions under the Crown.
End the separate administration and establish direct colonial rule.
The Raad beneath the Union Jack

The imperial delegates have chosen to preserve a separate Transvaal administration. Our farms and towns remain within its borders, but the treaty reserves foreign policy to Britain and replaces the republic's sovereign authority with Crown supervision. District officials must now explain the settlement to burghers who supplied horses, rifles and provisions to the commandos. Their acceptance cannot be presumed: the memory of the republic survives in the same communities the new government must govern. Yet maintaining the local raad offers a means of settling accounts and rebuilding public services without placing every district directly under distant colonial officials. The extraordinary mobilisation is over, the difficult work of governing after defeat begins.
Preserve the district institutions and begin rebuilding.
An Inland Transvaal under the Crown

Britain's settlement separates the inland administration from its eastern acquisitions. Those South Mozambique districts still held by Transvaal pass directly to imperial control, the remaining country continues as British Transvaal. The ports and routes towards the Indian Ocean that promised an independent outlet will now answer to British officials. Boer delegates have preserved a government for the interior, but they return to Pretoria with a treaty that limits both its sovereignty and its access to the sea. Merchants must renegotiate their arrangements, while district leaders confront the anger of men who fought to keep those roads open.
Keep the inland administration alive, despite the loss of the eastern districts.
The End of Separate Transvaal Administration

The Crown has decided to abolish the separate administration of British Transvaal. Its treasury, troops and remaining districts will pass directly to Britain. Imperial officials present integration as a remedy for overlapping authority and the expense of maintaining another government, the burghers see the disappearance of the institutions through which they defended local self-rule. Republican claims will remain, and annexation will increase resentment among the Boer population. Direct administration therefore begins with a political dispute, not with the effortless conversion of the country into a loyal colony. If you govern British Transvaal, accepting this outcome transfers your play to Britain before the country is incorporated, allowing the campaign to continue under the victorious administration.
Complete the incorporation and establish Crown administration.
Transvaal: A Colony to Govern

Dispatches from Pretoria announce the end of the separate Transvaal administration. The victory has enlarged Britain's direct possessions and strengthened the imperial position in southern Africa, but a proclamation cannot by itself produce a functioning colony. Magistrates must settle wartime accounts, maintain roads and collect revenue in districts whose burghers remember a different government. The colonial office now carries those responsibilities directly. Republican claims remain in the incorporated territory, and the resentment caused by annexation will require patient administration as well as a credible military presence. London may celebrate the settlement as an imperial success, its lasting value will depend on how the new possessions are governed after the celebrations have ended.
Publish the settlement and assume the responsibilities of direct rule.
The Colonial Office Considers Integration

Five years have passed since the Pretoria settlement placed Transvaal under the Crown. Reconstruction has received imperial funding, and the separate administration is at peace. Officials now propose replacing that government with direct colonial rule. Integration would remove an intermediary between London and the districts, but it would also transfer the cost of administration to Britain and extinguish institutions that have helped contain opposition since the war. The proposal requires a further investment of 10,000 pounds. Republican claims would remain, and Boer resentment would rise when the change is enacted. Ministers must decide whether the advantages of direct control justify reopening a political question that the original treaty deliberately left unsettled.
Invest 10,000 pounds and proceed with incorporation.
Keep the separate administration, reconsider after another year.
Rebuilding after the Pretoria Settlement

The imperial government has approved funds for the recovery of British Transvaal. War has disrupted the ordinary work on which the districts depend: farms need supplies, mining operations need reliable transport, and officials must restore the accounts through which local services are paid. Part of the appropriation reaches our treasury directly, the remainder supports a five-year programme of administration and agricultural and mining recovery. Reconstruction does not restore the republic's independence, but it gives the government a practical answer to communities asking what the settlement has achieved beyond a change of flag. Fair distribution will matter as much as the total expenditure, especially where the burdens of the campaign fell unevenly.
Apply the grant to district recovery and public administration.
District Institutions within the Imperial Settlement

Britain has authorised a measure of district autonomy within the existing Crown settlement. Local institutions will have a recognised role in ordinary administration, while foreign policy and the republic's subordinate status remain unchanged. For the burghers, this offers a way to address disputes through familiar officials instead of treating every decision as an imposition from outside. For the imperial government, it is an attempt to secure cooperation without reopening the question of sovereignty. The arrangement improves administrative confidence and reduces Boer resentment, though greater political awareness accompanies the restoration of a local voice. Its success will depend on respecting the limits promised in the settlement and on whether officials can make those institutions work in practice.
Restore a local voice within the Crown administration.
Fund Reconstruction in British Transvaal

Appropriate 5,000 pounds for recovery under the Pretoria settlement. British Transvaal receives 2,000 pounds and five years of improved administration, farming and mining efficiency. This programme is required before later integration can be considered.
Recognise Transvaal District Institutions

Invest 2,000 pounds in a local administrative settlement. British Transvaal remains a Crown dependency, but its district institutions receive lasting recognition, improving administration and attraction to immigrants while reducing Boer resentment.
Consider Integrating British Transvaal

After five years under the Pretoria settlement and funded reconstruction, consider replacing the separate administration with direct colonial rule. Both countries must be at peace and the dependency must control its territory. The conference offers incorporation for 10,000 pounds or a one-year postponement, annexation preserves republican claims and brings resistance.
Victory at Pretoria
The conference has reinforced imperial prestige for five years.
The Pretoria Administrative Settlement
The separate administration is protected from the new integration decision for five years after the treaty.
Crown Administration Restored
The settlement supports the recovery of local administration for five years.
The Cost of Direct Transvaal Rule
Britain bears the administrative and revenue costs of integration for five years.
Integration under Review
Ministers have postponed reconsideration of direct rule for one year.
Imperial Reconstruction Programme
Five years of funded administrative, farming and mining recovery.
Recognised District Institutions
Local institutions retain a voice within the dependency, supporting administration and immigration.
